title: Minimum Window Substring — sliding window with frequency map.
shortTitle: Minimum Window Substring — Sliding Window With Frequency Map

s1_definition.profdef: The Minimum Window Substring problem finds the shortest contiguous substring of a source string that contains all characters of a target string, including duplicates. The sliding-window solution expands the right edge until the window covers all required characters, then contracts the left edge as far as possible while still covering them, recording the smallest valid window. It runs in linear time using a frequency map of required characters and a satisfied-count.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India scans a long string of transaction codes and must find the shortest stretch that contains a required set of codes, each the right number of times, perhaps to locate the tightest segment covering a mandatory checklist. You grow a window on the right until it contains everything required, then you tighten it from the left as much as possible while it still satisfies the checklist, and you keep the tightest satisfying window found.
s1_definition.oneliner: Expand right until the window has everything needed, then shrink left while it still does, tracking the smallest.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Minimum Window Substring problem finds the shortest contiguous substring of a source string that contains all characters of a target string, including duplicates. The sliding-window solution expands the right edge until the window covers all required characters, then contracts the left edge as far as possible while still covering them, recording the smallest valid window. It runs in linear time using a frequency map of required characters and a satisfied-count.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India scans a long string of transaction codes and must find the shortest stretch that contains a required set of codes, each the right number of times, perhaps to locate the tightest segment covering a mandatory checklist. You grow a window on the right until it contains everything required, then you tighten it from the left as much as possible while it still satisfies the checklist, and you keep the tightest satisfying window found.

**One line to remember:** Expand right until the window has everything needed, then shrink left while it still does, tracking the smallest.

sections.s2_technical:
You need two ideas: a way to know what the target requires, and a way to know when the current window satisfies it. The target's requirements are a frequency map, how many of each character are needed. The window tracks how many of those requirements are currently met. A compact way is to keep a counter of how many distinct required characters are fully satisfied in the window, and compare it to the number of distinct required characters.

You keep a need map from character to required count, and a have map or a window count. You move the right index forward, and for each character you add it to the window; if it is a required character and the window's count for it just reached the needed count, you increment a formed counter. When formed equals the number of distinct required characters, the window is valid, meaning it contains all requirements. At that point you try to shrink: while the window is still valid, you record its length if it is the smallest so far, then remove the character at the left index, advance left, and if removing a required character drops its window count below the needed count, you decrement formed, which ends the shrink.

The reason this is linear is the same amortized argument as other sliding windows: the right index moves forward across the whole string once, and the left index also only moves forward, never backward, so each character is added once and removed at most once. The formed counter lets you test validity in constant time per step instead of rescanning the window.

A senior point is handling duplicate requirements correctly. If the target needs two of a character, the formed counter must only increment when the window's count reaches exactly the needed two, not on the first occurrence, and must only decrement when shrinking drops it below two. Using the equality check at the exact threshold, rather than a mere presence check, is what makes duplicates work. Many buggy versions use a set and silently fail when the target has repeats.

Another senior point is the result tracking and the no-answer case. You record the best window as a start index and a length, updating only when a strictly smaller valid window appears, and if no valid window is ever formed you return an empty string. For an open character set you use HashMaps; for a fixed small alphabet arrays are faster. In banking I note the target may be larger than any window, so the empty result must be clean.

A small finance-domain example: `need` built from the target, `formed` counting satisfied requirements, expanding right and contracting left while `formed == required`, recording the minimal start and length, returns the tightest covering segment.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India has a long log of single-character transaction codes and must find the shortest contiguous stretch that contains a mandatory set of codes with required multiplicities, for example the tightest window that includes at least one debit, two credits, and one transfer, to locate the most compact compliant segment. The log is long, so the search must be linear. Finding the minimum window substring is exactly this.

This is exactly how Minimum Window Substring works in Java — expanding the right edge until the window covers all required codes, then contracting the left edge while it still does.

Problem 2 — The target may require duplicates, such as two credits, so the satisfaction check must respect counts, not mere presence, and the required set may never fit, in which case the result is empty. This shows the duplicate-count handling and the no-answer edge case.

What the code will do: a `MinWindowFinder` with `minWindow(String source, String target)` using a sliding window with a need map and a formed counter. The demo finds the tightest covering window for a code log and target.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the source code log `ADOBECODEBANC` and the target `ABC`, requiring one A, one B, and one C.

Step 1: the need map is A one, B one, C one, so required is three. We expand right, adding each character to the window. By the time the right edge reaches the first `C` at index five, the window `ADOBEC` contains one A, one B, and one C, so formed reaches three and the window is valid.

Step 2: now we contract from the left while valid. The window `ADOBEC` has length six. We remove `A` at index zero; the window's A count drops below the needed one, so formed drops to two and the shrink stops, with left now at one. The best window so far is `ADOBEC` length six.

Step 3: we keep expanding right. As more characters arrive, the window regains the missing A when a later A appears, formed returns to three, and we contract again, each time recording a smaller valid window if found. Through the middle of the string the tightest valid windows get shorter as the required characters cluster.

Step 4: near the end, the right edge reaches the final `C` in the tail `BANC`. At that point the window can be contracted down to exactly `BANC`, which contains one B, one A, and one C, a length of four, which is smaller than any previous valid window, so the best becomes `BANC`.

Step 5: the scan finishes with the best window `BANC` of length four, returned as the answer. For the target `CC` on `DCCTC`, the tightest window covering two C characters is the adjacent `CC`. For the target `ABC` on `DD`, no window ever forms all three, so formed never reaches three and the result is the empty string.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T21:40:00Z INFO Minimum window = 'BANC'
2026-10-26T21:40:00Z INFO Window = 'BANC'
2026-10-26T21:40:00Z INFO Minimum window = 'CC'
2026-10-26T21:40:00Z INFO Window = 'CC'
2026-10-26T21:40:00Z INFO Minimum window = ''
2026-10-26T21:40:00Z INFO Window = ''
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Source: "ADOBECODEBANC"  Target: "ABC"  need{A:1,B:1,C:1} required=3
    │
    ▼
  expand right until formed==required; then contract left while valid
    │ right→'C'(5): window "ADOBEC" formed=3 → record len6; shrink to left=1
    │ ... later tail "BANC" formed=3 → len4 < 6 → best="BANC"
    ▼
  best window = "BANC"   (target "CC" → "CC" ; unreachable → "")
    ▼
  Output: shortest covering substring
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Minimum Window Substring finds the shortest contiguous substring of a source that contains all characters of a target, including duplicates, and I solve it with an expand-and-contract sliding window in linear time. I build a need map of how many of each character the target requires, and I track how many distinct requirements the current window fully satisfies with a formed counter. I expand the right edge until formed equals the number of distinct required characters, meaning the window covers everything, then I contract the left edge as far as possible while it stays valid, recording the smallest valid window.

The amortized-linear argument is the same as other sliding windows: the right index sweeps the string once and the left index only moves forward, so each character is added once and removed at most once, and the formed counter lets me check validity in constant time instead of rescanning the window each step.

The detail that separates a correct solution from a common buggy one is duplicate requirements. If the target needs two of a character, I increment formed only when the window's count reaches exactly the needed two, and decrement it only when contracting drops it below two, using an exact-threshold equality check rather than a mere presence test. A version that uses a set instead of counts silently fails whenever the target has repeats. I also track the best window as a start and length, returning an empty string cleanly when no valid window ever forms.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on long transaction-code logs to locate the tightest contiguous segment containing a mandatory set of codes with required multiplicities, such as the most compact stretch covering a compliance checklist. Explaining the need map and formed counter, the amortized-linear sweep, and especially the exact-count handling of duplicates shows the interviewer that I understand the hardest sliding-window problem rather than a simplified presence-only version.
